A write-ahead log, also known to as a redo log in some databases, is a record of all changes made to the database. When you insert, update, or delete a record in most databases, the database first writes the change to the log before updating the actual data. This way, if the system crashes, the database can recovery the transaction by simply replaying it. This is known as a redo operation.

The write-ahead log consists of a log of all transactions since the last checkpoint. A checkpoint is a point in time when the database is fully synced to the underlying storage, which means the transaction log is flushed and written to storage. This allows the database to recover the state of the database at that point in time in case of a crash.

When a crash occurs, the database can recover by undoing incomplete transactions and replaying committed transactions. The database looks at the transactions in the log, identifies the transactions that were not completed during the crash, and reverts them. The committed transactions are replayed, allowing the database to recover to the point in time just before the crash.

## Step 1: Introduction to Write-Ahead Logging
A write-ahead log (WAL) is a mechanism used by databases to ensure data integrity and facilitate recovery in the event of a system failure or crash. It involves recording every transaction before it is applied to the main database, thus ensuring that none of the transaction's effects are lost in the case of a crash.

## Step 2: Operation of Write-Ahead Logging
When a transaction is initiated, the database first writes a log record with metadata about the transaction, such as the transaction ID, the type of transaction (insert, delete, update), and any relevant data before it makes any changes to the database. This log record is essentially a "record of intent" to make these changes. If the transaction is completed successfully, the database then writes the actual changes to the database files. If the transaction is rolled back due to a failure or user decision, the database simply discards the changes made to the database and removes the corresponding log record. However, if the system crashes before the transaction can be completed, the log can be used to restore the database to a consistent state.
